3.1.1.locator: S3 user guide 'Protecting data in transit with encryption' (TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 supported across all API endpoints); AWS announcement 'TLS 1.2 to become the minimum TLS protocol level for all AWS API endpoints' (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/tls-1-2-required-for-aws-endpoints/): as of 2024-02-27 all AWS service API endpoints require minimum TLS 1.2, TLS 1.0/1.1 deprecated
3.1.1.notes: TLS 1.2 is the enforced floor on all AWS service API endpoints; TLS 1.3 is supported and negotiated where the client allows (AWS recommends 1.3, current SDKs default to it). 'TLS 1.2' selected as the guaranteed standard; note the 1.3 support in the cell comment if the form allows. Sources are AWS documentation/announcements surfaced in domain-restricted search; direct fetch blocked.

3.1.2.locator: S3 user guide, server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3): 'uses 256-bit Advanced Encryption Standard Galois/Counter Mode (AES-GCM)' / 'one of the strongest block ciphers available, 256-bit Advanced Encryption Standard (AES-256)'; all new S3 object uploads encrypted by default since 2023-01-05
3.1.2.notes: Documented as AES-256-GCM; encryption at rest is on by default for S3 (where Tavus-stored recordings/media would live). Source text from AWS docs search snippets; direct fetch blocked by gateway.

3.1.3.locator: AWS Backup developer guide, 'Encryption for backups in AWS Backup': 'When AWS Backup independently encrypts a backup, it uses the industry-standard AES-256 encryption algorithm', controlled via the AWS KMS key on the backup vault; cross-account/cross-Region copies automatically encrypted
3.1.3.notes: Scope caveat: this documents the AWS Backup service (customer-configured backups AES-256 via KMS) and backups of encrypted source resources inherit encryption. AWS does not publish a single statement covering every internal backup path, so treat as low confidence and confirm Tavus's actual backup configuration; falling back to 'Not known' would also be defensible. Snippet-sourced; direct fetch blocked.

3.1.4.locator: S3 SSE-S3 documentation: 'Amazon S3 encrypts each object with a unique key. As an additional safeguard, it encrypts the key itself with a key that it rotates regularly' - default keys are generated and managed by AWS
3.1.4.notes: Default managed-cloud answer per the field playbook. AWS also offers customer-managed KMS keys (SSE-KMS/CMK) and customer-provided keys (SSE-C/BYOK); if Tavus uses customer-managed KMS keys for its buckets, the correct dropdown flips to 'Key generated by your company' - HUMAN MUST CONFIRM Tavus's actual key configuration before the cell is written.

3.1.6.notes: AWS is IaaS: under the shared-responsibility model AWS does not act on the content of customer data, and no AWS primary source retrieved states that AWS (as processor) anonymizes customer personal data. AWS documents tooling customers can use to build anonymization/pseudonymization themselves (Navigating GDPR Compliance on AWS whitepaper, docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/navigating-gdpr-compliance/), but that is customer-operated, not a subprocessor capability. Searched: aws.amazon.com/compliance/gdpr-center/, docs.aws.amazon.com navigating-gdpr-compliance whitepaper pages (all direct fetches blocked by gateway 403; domain-restricted search snippets showed no statement that AWS itself anonymizes).

3.1.7.notes: Same reasoning as 3.1.6: pseudonymization on AWS is documented as a customer-built/customer-operated pattern (e.g. AWS whitepaper and reference architectures), not as something AWS performs on customer data as a processor. No primary-source statement found that AWS the subprocessor pseudonymizes customer personal data. Searched the same AWS GDPR pages as 3.1.6.
